reading.title: When the Tool Starts Creating
paragraphs: Creative tools have always changed what artists can make. Photography altered painting; synthesizers changed music; digital editing transformed film. Generative AI is different in one important respect: it can produce finished-looking text, images, audio, and video in response to a short instruction. The tool is no longer merely changing a brushstroke or correcting a colour; it can participate in the apparent production of the creative material itself.

This creates genuine opportunities. A designer can generate variations rapidly, a filmmaker can visualise scenes before shooting, and a writer can test alternative structures. People with limited technical skill may be able to express ideas that they previously could not execute. UNESCO has noted that AI is reshaping cultural production, distribution, access, and audience engagement, while also raising questions about authorship, ownership, and creative agency.

The concern is not simply that AI can produce attractive work. It is how it learns. Generative systems are trained on large amounts of existing material, which means their outputs draw statistically from patterns in human-created culture. Critics argue that this can blur the line between inspiration and uncredited appropriation, particularly when creators did not consent to their work being used for training. Others respond that human creativity also builds on existing styles, conventions, and influences, although the scale and mechanism are clearly different.

There is also an economic dimension. AI can reduce the cost of producing routine creative material, which may help small organisations but threaten some paid creative work. At the same time, new roles may emerge around direction, curation, editing, and hybrid human–AI production.

The hardest question is therefore not whether AI is “creative” in the same way as a person. It is what happens to human creativity when generating a plausible first result becomes almost effortless. Perhaps creativity becomes more about choosing, refining, combining, and giving meaning. Or perhaps easy generation encourages a flood of derivative work and makes distinctive human expression more valuable.

There is also a difference between generating and judging. Producing ten plausible images in seconds does not tell a creator which one communicates the right idea, fits a cultural context, avoids harmful stereotypes, or deserves to exist at all. If generation becomes cheap, selection and editorial judgment may become more valuable. That possibility complicates simple predictions that AI either “replaces” creativity or merely serves as another neutral tool.
AI may simultaneously lower the barrier to making content and raise the bar for producing work that feels genuinely worth attention.

inShort.summary: Generative AI can expand **creative agency** by helping people explore ideas quickly, but it complicates **authorship**, **originality**, and the economic value of creative work. Because models **draw from** existing culture, they can **blur the line** between inspiration and appropriation while also helping creators **build on** ideas in new ways.

reading.title: Recognition, Surveillance, and the Problem of Scale
paragraphs: Facial-recognition systems compare images of faces in order to verify or identify people. The technology can serve relatively narrow purposes—unlocking a device, checking a passport, or confirming that one person matches one stored identity. It can also be used at a much larger scale, such as searching camera footage against databases of faces.

Supporters point to potential benefits in security, missing-person searches, border processing, or identifying a suspect from evidence. In some contexts, faster identification could reduce manual work and help authorities focus an investigation.

The concerns become more serious when recognition turns into continuous surveillance. A person walking through a public square traditionally does not have to identify themselves to every camera they pass. Large-scale facial recognition can change that expectation by making identification possible at a distance and without active consent.

Accuracy also matters. NIST has documented demographic differentials in face-recognition performance across many algorithms, including differences in false-positive and false-negative rates associated with age, sex, and race. Its ongoing evaluations also show that systems vary substantially, and image quality can affect performance. This makes statements such as “facial recognition is biased” too broad: performance depends on the specific algorithm, task, data, and conditions. But it also means decision-makers cannot assume that a high average accuracy guarantees equal performance for every population.

Even a small false-positive rate can matter when a system scans millions of people. If a match leads only to a second check, the consequence is different from a system where a match directly causes arrest, denial of access, or inclusion on a watchlist.

The policy question is therefore not simply whether the technology “works.” It involves purpose, proportionality, consent, accuracy, oversight, data retention, and what happens after a match. The same tool can be relatively low-risk in one setting and far more intrusive in another.

Governance also has to consider function creep. A database created for one narrow purpose can later be connected to other systems or used for broader monitoring. Even when the original use appears proportionate, expanding access can change the risk profile. Clear retention periods, audit logs, independent review, and rules about secondary use therefore matter alongside raw accuracy.

Public acceptance may also depend on whether a system is visible and contestable. A person who is wrongly matched needs a practical route to challenge the result and correct records. Without that, a technical error can become an administrative problem that follows someone beyond the original scan.
The difficult task is deciding which uses are proportionate to the benefit claimed—and which uses turn ordinary public movement into routine identification.

inShort.summary: Facial recognition is a form of **biometric** identification whose risks depend heavily on context. **Surveillance**, a **false positive**, or a **demographic differential** may have serious consequences when systems are used at scale, so debates often centre on **proportionality**, consent, and whether people can realistically **opt out**.

reading.title: Flexible Work, Uneven Risk
paragraphs: Digital labour platforms have changed how people find work. A driver can log on to an app, a designer can accept a project from another country, and a delivery worker can choose when to start or stop taking orders. For some workers, this flexibility is the main attraction. Platform work can provide additional income, allow people to combine work with study or family responsibilities, and connect workers with clients they would never otherwise reach.

The same flexibility can also transfer risk from the organisation to the worker. A traditional employee may receive predictable pay, paid leave, social insurance, and clearer procedures for discipline or dismissal. A platform worker may have fluctuating income, unpaid waiting time, limited social protection, and little control over changes to the algorithm that allocates work.

ILO research has repeatedly highlighted this tension. Its studies of digital labour platforms examine pay, work availability, intensity, social protection, and work–life balance. A 2026 ILO brief also emphasised how difficult it remains to measure the global number of platform workers accurately, while recent country studies continue to report both income opportunities and problems such as long hours, uncertainty, and gaps in protection.

Employment classification is central to the debate. If a platform worker is genuinely independent, the freedom to choose clients and hours may justify a different relationship from standard employment. But if the platform sets prices, controls access to customers, monitors performance, and can deactivate the worker’s account, critics ask how independent that worker really is.

Consumers and businesses are part of the system too. Customers value fast, affordable services. Platforms argue that rigid employment models could reduce flexibility or raise prices. Workers may themselves disagree: some want employee protections, while others fear losing autonomy.

Another complication is that flexibility itself has more than one form. Choosing when to log in is valuable, but it is not the same as being able to set prices, reject work without penalty, build a portable client base, or understand how ratings affect future opportunities. A worker can have schedule flexibility while remaining highly dependent on one platform for income.

Portability is another issue. Ratings, customer histories, and reputation may be valuable assets for workers, but they often remain inside one platform. If workers cannot take those records elsewhere, changing platforms can mean starting from zero, which can reduce practical independence even when formal contracts describe them as self-employed.

The gig economy therefore does not fit neatly into “good jobs” or “bad jobs.” The key question is who controls the work, who carries the risk, and whether flexibility is genuinely chosen—or simply the only available way to earn.

inShort.summary: Platform work can offer **flexibility**, but it can also create **precarity** when income and hours are uncertain. Debates focus on **employment classification**, **social protection**, and **algorithmic management**, especially when workers must **piece together** income while remaining **at the mercy of** platform rules.

reading.title: When the Workday Has No Clear End
paragraphs: Digital communication has made work more flexible, but it has also made employees easier to reach. A message can arrive at 10 p.m., a manager can check a team chat on Sunday, and remote workers may pass their laptop every time they enter the living room. The physical boundary between “at work” and “not at work” has become easier to blur.

The “right to disconnect” generally refers to workers being able to disengage from work-related electronic communication during non-working time without negative consequences. The idea is not necessarily that no message can ever be sent after hours; rather, employees should not be expected to remain permanently available unless their role genuinely requires it.

The ILO has highlighted the importance of boundary management in telework and has discussed the ability to disconnect as one way to protect work–life balance. The concern is cumulative. A single five-minute message may seem harmless, but repeated interruptions can make personal time feel conditional and can create an always-on expectation.

A universal rule is difficult, however. Hospitals, emergency services, global teams, senior executives, and workers with flexible schedules may need different arrangements. Some employees prefer to take two hours off in the afternoon and answer messages later. A rigid “no contact after 6 p.m.” policy could reduce that flexibility.

Enforcement raises another issue. If managers officially say there is no expectation to reply but reward employees who respond immediately at night, the culture may contradict the written policy. Effective disconnection therefore depends not only on law or company rules but on workload, staffing, leadership behaviour, and performance expectations.

There is also a collective-action problem. One employee may personally choose not to answer late messages, but that choice becomes harder if colleagues who remain available gain better assignments or faster promotion. In that environment, an “individual choice” can create pressure on everyone. Organisational norms matter because workers often compare their behaviour with what seems rewarded around them.

A useful distinction is between sending and expecting. A global team may need messages to be sent across time zones while still allowing the receiver to answer during their own working hours. Delayed delivery tools, status indicators, and explicit escalation rules can protect flexibility without requiring the whole organisation to work on one clock.

The debate is ultimately about time sovereignty: how much control should workers have over the boundary between paid work and the rest of life? A workable policy has to protect rest without assuming that every profession, worker, or time zone follows the same schedule.

inShort.summary: A right to disconnect aims to protect the **boundary** between work and private life by reducing **after-hours** expectations and constant **availability**. Yet flexible schedules can **blur the boundaries**, and some roles require employees to **be on call**, so the challenge is to **draw a line** without creating an inflexible rule.

reading.title: Treating One Patient—or Changing Future Generations?
paragraphs: Gene-editing tools such as CRISPR have made it possible to change DNA with a precision that would have seemed extraordinary a few decades ago. The phrase “gene editing,” however, covers several very different activities, and ethical discussion becomes confused when they are treated as one thing.

Somatic editing changes cells in an existing patient without intending the change to be inherited by future children. This approach is already being used in approved therapies for certain genetic disorders. The ethical questions are serious but familiar: safety, effectiveness, access, informed consent, and cost.

Heritable genome editing is different. It involves changes that could be passed to future generations. An intervention intended to prevent one severe inherited disease could therefore affect people who did not—and could not—consent, as well as descendants who may inherit both the intended change and any unintended consequences.

The World Health Organization distinguishes somatic, germline, and heritable editing and has emphasised the need for robust national and international governance. WHO has stated that clinical applications of human germline genome editing should not proceed prematurely, reflecting both unresolved scientific uncertainty and broader ethical concerns.

Supporters of carefully controlled future use argue that there may be rare cases where editing could prevent catastrophic disease when other reproductive options cannot provide an unaffected embryo. Critics respond that safety is only one part of the issue. Once heritable editing becomes acceptable for disease, societies may face pressure to expand it toward reducing ordinary health risks or selecting non-medical traits.

This is where the treatment-versus-enhancement distinction becomes difficult. Preventing a fatal disorder appears very different from selecting height or appearance, but many traits lie between those extremes.

Uncertainty is especially important because genetic changes can differ in reversibility. Editing cells in one patient affects that patient; a heritable change could be passed to descendants who did not consent and whose risks may be difficult to predict. That does not settle the ethical question, but it raises the evidentiary threshold and makes long-term monitoring more important.

Access adds a further layer. If a safe and effective intervention were extremely expensive, the ethical debate would extend beyond whether it should exist to who could receive it. A technology that prevents severe disease could reduce suffering while also widening inequality if availability followed wealth rather than medical need.

The debate therefore requires more precision than “editing DNA is good” or “editing DNA is wrong.” It asks which cells are changed, for what purpose, with what evidence, who bears the risk, what alternatives exist, and whether a decision made today can legitimately shape people who will exist generations from now.

inShort.summary: **Somatic** gene editing affects an existing patient, while **heritable** editing could **pass on** changes to future generations. The therapeutic goal may be compelling, but **unintended consequences** and the possibility of **opening the door to** non-medical **enhancement** make the ethical boundary difficult to **pin down**.

reading.title: The Feed That Learns You
paragraphs: Personalised systems are designed to predict relevance. If you repeatedly watch a certain type of video, follow particular creators, or ignore certain topics, a platform can use those signals to shape what appears next. This can make an information feed feel efficient and personally useful.

The concern is that relevance can become repetition. If a user already prefers one interpretation of a topic, an algorithm optimised for engagement may continue offering similar material. Over time, the user may receive less exposure to unfamiliar views and gain the impression that their own perspective is more widely shared or more obviously correct than it really is. This is often described through terms such as “filter bubble” or “echo chamber.”

However, the causal story is more complicated than “algorithm causes belief.” People actively choose friends, media sources, communities, and search terms. Confirmation bias—the tendency to notice or favour information consistent with existing beliefs—predates social media. A user can reject recommendations, search for opposing views, or follow diverse sources. Offline communities also shape opinions.

Researchers and experts continue to debate how strong algorithmic effects are in different contexts. Pew’s work on algorithmic systems has highlighted concerns that personalised categorisation can deepen divides and reduce serendipitous exposure, while more recent digital-market analysis from the OECD emphasises how platforms shape choice through data-driven mechanisms. Neither point proves that algorithms mechanically determine what users believe.

A further complication is that recommendations may expose users to material they would never have found independently. Someone interested in one topic can discover experts, cultures, arguments, or niche communities from around the world.

The useful question is therefore not whether personalisation creates a perfect informational prison. It is how much control users have over what enters and leaves their feed, whether systems reward extreme engagement, and whether platforms make diverse exploration easy or inconvenient.

Exposure is also not the same as persuasion. Seeing more of one viewpoint may strengthen it, provoke resistance, or have little effect at all. People bring existing identities, social networks, habits, and offline experiences into the feed. This is why evidence about algorithmic effects should distinguish what the system shows, what users choose, and what ultimately changes their beliefs or behaviour.

Control tools can matter even when their effects are modest. Being able to reset recommendations, request chronological ordering, hide topics, or ask why something was shown gives users ways to interrupt the loop. Whether people actually use those controls is a separate question from whether meaningful control is available.
An algorithm may reinforce a preference, but that preference also teaches the algorithm what to reinforce. The relationship is a feedback loop rather than a one-way force.

inShort.summary: Personalisation can create a **feedback loop** in which a user’s choices **reinforce** what an algorithm recommends. This may reduce **serendipity** and amplify **confirmation bias**, but users can still **seek out** different sources, **tune out** recommendations, and deliberately **broaden their horizons**.

reading.title: Can More Output Mean Less Damage?
paragraphs: Economic growth is usually measured by increases in the value of goods and services produced. Historically, growth has often been associated with higher energy use, greater extraction of materials, and more pollution. That history leads to an obvious concern: if economies keep expanding, can environmental pressure keep falling?

One answer is “decoupling.” Relative decoupling occurs when environmental harm grows more slowly than the economy. Absolute decoupling is stronger: the economy grows while a particular environmental pressure, such as carbon emissions, actually falls.

Evidence shows that this can happen in important areas. OECD analysis has documented periods in which GDP growth decoupled from greenhouse-gas emissions in many member countries. Cleaner electricity, energy efficiency, structural economic change, and environmental regulation can all contribute. This means the relationship between growth and emissions is not mechanically fixed.

However, critics point out that reducing domestic carbon emissions does not automatically mean reducing every form of environmental pressure. Material use, biodiversity loss, land use, water stress, imported goods, and pollution can move differently. A wealthy country may also consume goods produced elsewhere, shifting part of the environmental footprint rather than eliminating it.

Technology can improve efficiency, but rebound effects matter. A car that uses half as much fuel per kilometre reduces fuel use if driving stays constant; if lower costs encourage much more driving, some of the expected environmental gain may disappear.

The debate is therefore partly about what “growth” consists of. Growth based on more fossil fuel, land conversion, and material extraction creates different pressures from growth in digital services, healthcare, education, repair, or renewable energy. Yet even low-material sectors require infrastructure and energy.

Measurement boundaries therefore matter. Territorial emissions count what is released inside a country, while consumption-based measures can also reflect emissions embodied in imported goods. Neither measure answers every question, but comparing them can reveal whether apparent environmental improvement comes from cleaner production, structural change, or shifting production abroad.

Time scale matters as well. An economy can improve carbon intensity—the emissions produced per unit of output—while total emissions remain high because economic activity grows faster than efficiency improves. Relative improvement is meaningful, but it is not automatically sufficient when an environmental target is defined in absolute terms.

The question is not answered by pointing to one country where emissions fell or one resource that became more efficient. The demanding test is whether economies can improve living standards while reducing total environmental pressures fast enough, across multiple dimensions, and without simply moving the damage elsewhere.

inShort.summary: **Decoupling** occurs when economic output and environmental pressure move apart, but **absolute decoupling** is a stronger test than simple efficiency. Policies can **phase out** damaging technologies and **scale up** cleaner ones, yet **rebound effects**, imported impacts, and other **externalities** can complicate claims of sustainable growth.

reading.title: A Tool That Multiplies Opportunity—and Advantage
paragraphs: Technology can lower barriers dramatically. A student in a small town can attend an online course from another country. A small business can reach customers worldwide. Telemedicine can connect patients with specialists, and digital payments can provide services without a nearby bank branch. These examples support the idea that technology can spread opportunity.

But access is not evenly distributed. According to the International Telecommunication Union’s 2025 estimates, roughly three-quarters of the world’s population were online, leaving about 2.2 billion people offline. Coverage has expanded, yet affordability, quality, skills, gender gaps, and urban–rural differences continue to shape how much people can actually benefit.

This illustrates why the “digital divide” is not simply a line between people who have internet and people who do not. Two students may both be technically connected, while one has a private laptop, fast broadband, digital skills, and a quiet room and the other relies on a shared phone and expensive mobile data. Equal access in a narrow sense can still produce unequal outcomes.

New technologies can also reward people who already possess complementary advantages. An AI assistant may increase productivity most for people with the education to evaluate its output, reliable infrastructure, and jobs that allow them to use it. Businesses with more data and computing resources may adopt advanced systems faster than smaller competitors.

At the same time, technology can help people catch up. Translation, accessibility tools, low-cost online learning, and remote work can reduce barriers that once excluded people from information or employment.

The effect therefore depends on distribution. A technology that makes an opportunity cheaper may reduce inequality if disadvantaged groups can actually use it. The same technology may widen gaps if the benefits flow mainly to people who already have money, skills, networks, and infrastructure.

Timing matters too. New technologies are often expensive, difficult to use, or concentrated in particular organisations before they become cheaper and more widespread. An innovation can therefore widen gaps in the short term and narrow them later—or do the reverse if early advantages compound. Evaluating inequality requires asking not only whether access expands, but how quickly benefits diffuse and who captures the gains during the transition.

The relevant inequality may also change. A translation tool can reduce a language barrier while increasing the advantage of people who know how to verify its mistakes. Cheap online courses can expand access while making credentials, mentoring, and professional networks more important differentiators. Technology can close one gap and expose another.
Technological progress does not arrive on a level playing field. It changes the field—and sometimes makes existing differences more valuable.

inShort.summary: The **digital divide** involves not only **access** but also **affordability**, skills, and infrastructure. Technology can help disadvantaged groups **catch up** and governments can try to **bridge the gap**, but unequal resources may cause some people to be **left behind** even when everyone appears connected.

reading.title: When “The Algorithm Did It” Is Not an Answer
paragraphs: Suppose an AI system denies a person a loan, recommends the wrong medical treatment, or incorrectly flags a worker as fraudulent. When harm occurs, saying “the algorithm made the decision” does not resolve responsibility. An AI system is created, trained, supplied, configured, deployed, monitored, and used by people and organisations.

This creates a chain of responsibility. Developers decide architecture and training methods. Data suppliers influence what information the system learns from. A vendor chooses what claims to make about performance. The organisation deploying the system decides where to use it, what level of risk is acceptable, and whether a human reviews the output. Individual employees may then rely on or override the result.

The OECD AI Principles state that AI actors should be accountable based on their roles, context, and ability to act, and they emphasise traceability and ongoing risk management. UNESCO similarly states that AI systems should not displace ultimate human responsibility and accountability.

That sounds clear in principle, but real systems are complex. A hospital may use software produced by one company, built partly on a model from another provider and trained on data gathered elsewhere. A harmful outcome can emerge from interactions rather than one obvious mistake.

Human oversight can also become symbolic. If a worker must approve hundreds of automated decisions quickly and lacks the information or authority to challenge them, calling that person “human in the loop” may not create meaningful control.

Accountability therefore depends on traceability: organisations need enough records to reconstruct what happened, which system version was used, what data or rules mattered, and who had authority to intervene. Independent auditing may be necessary in high-impact contexts.

Responsibility can also be divided by type. One actor may be responsible for preventing foreseeable technical failures, another for deciding whether the system is appropriate for a high-stakes setting, and another for responding when harm occurs. Separating design responsibility, deployment responsibility, and remedy can make accountability clearer than asking for one universal “owner” of every AI decision.

Remedy matters as much as blame. A person harmed by an automated decision may need an explanation, a correction, compensation, or a new decision process even when no individual acted maliciously. Accountability is therefore partly about creating routes to repair harm, not only identifying who should be punished.

The aim is not to find one person to blame for every failure. It is to prevent responsibility from falling through the cracks because each participant points to someone else. A well-governed system assigns duties before harm occurs rather than trying to invent them afterward.

inShort.summary: AI **accountability** requires clear **traceability**, meaningful human **oversight**, and duties across a **chain of responsibility**. In complex systems it can be difficult to **pin down** one cause, so organisations need audits and clear authority before responsibility can **fall through the cracks** or be casually **handed off** to “the algorithm.”

reading.title: The Privacy Choice That Is Not Really a Choice
paragraphs: Digital products often present privacy and convenience as a trade-off. Save your address and checkout becomes faster. Share your location and a map can predict your route. Allow a service to remember preferences and recommendations become more relevant. From this perspective, some data sharing is simply the price of a smoother experience.

Yet the trade-off is not always freely chosen. Interfaces can make the privacy-protective option difficult to find, require many extra steps, or use confusing language. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has described “dark patterns” as design practices that can subvert or impair consumer choice, including designs that steer people toward sharing more data than they intended.

Survey evidence also shows a gap between concern and behaviour. In a 2023 Pew study, 81% of U.S. adults said they were concerned about how companies use collected data, yet 56% said they often accepted privacy policies without reading them. This is sometimes described as a privacy paradox, but there are several possible explanations. People may value convenience more in the moment, may feel they have no realistic alternative, or may believe that reading a long policy would not give them meaningful control anyway.

That distinction matters. Choosing convenience after understanding the consequences is different from being pushed toward convenience by defaults and friction. A user might willingly share location with a navigation app during a journey while objecting to that information being retained for years or used for unrelated advertising.

Privacy itself is also not all-or-nothing. Systems can collect less data, process information on a device instead of centrally, delete it sooner, or offer paid versions with different business models.

Defaults deserve special attention because most users do not repeatedly redesign every service they use. A privacy-protective default can preserve convenience while reducing unnecessary collection; a data-intensive default can make disclosure feel inevitable. The practical power of the default means that “users can change it” is not always the same as saying both options are equally easy in real life.

Purpose limitation can narrow the conflict further. A user may reasonably provide location data for turn-by-turn navigation without expecting the same data to be reused for unrelated advertising or retained indefinitely. Asking what purpose a data point serves is often more informative than asking simply whether the user agreed to share it.

The better question may therefore be not “privacy or convenience?” but “How much data is genuinely necessary for this convenience, and how much additional collection is simply useful to the business?” Good design can sometimes reduce the trade-off instead of forcing users to choose between two extremes.

inShort.summary: The apparent **trade-off** between privacy and convenience can be distorted by **defaults**, interface **friction**, and **surveillance** business models. Users may **hand over** data because it is easier than trying to **opt out**, so a useful analysis asks where to **draw the line** and whether the service can be **streamlined** with less data.

reading.title: The Problem Hidden Inside “Merit”
paragraphs: Meritocracy sounds straightforward: positions and rewards should go to people according to ability and achievement rather than family background, wealth, or social connections. The appeal is obvious. If two people compete for the same opportunity, many of us instinctively want the outcome to reflect what they can do rather than who their parents are.

The difficulty begins with the word _merit_. Is merit natural talent? Hard work? Qualifications? Measurable results? The value someone creates for other people? These are not interchangeable. A gifted person who makes little effort and a less gifted person who works relentlessly may deserve recognition for different reasons. Even apparently objective measures, such as test scores or professional experience, are shaped by earlier opportunities.

This matters because people do not begin from the same **starting point**. An OECD analysis published in 2025 estimated that, across the OECD countries it examined, more than a quarter of inequality in household market income could be attributed to circumstances beyond an individual's control, such as parental socio-economic background, sex, and country of birth. Parental background was a particularly important factor. These estimates vary considerably between countries, and the analysis describes statistical patterns rather than proving that any one circumstance directly causes a particular person's outcome.

A defender of meritocracy might reply that unequal starting conditions do not make merit meaningless. Education, fair recruitment, transparent rules, and access to training can **level the playing field** without pretending that every difference can disappear. On this view, the aim is not perfect equality of outcomes but a system in which inherited advantage matters less and achievement matters more.

Critics raise a deeper objection. They argue that success itself can create advantages that are then passed to the next generation. A person who earns wealth through genuine achievement may naturally spend it on better housing, education, networks, and opportunities for their children. The next generation therefore starts from a different position. A system can reward merit at one stage and reproduce unequal opportunity at the next.

There is also a psychological problem. If society describes success entirely as deserved, successful people may underestimate the role of luck, support, or favourable circumstances. Those who struggle may be treated as if their situation reflects a personal failure even when structural barriers matter.

Even the attempt to correct unequal opportunity can create new disputes about fairness. Giving extra support to someone who faced greater barriers may improve substantive opportunity, while critics may see different treatment as inconsistent with equal rules. The disagreement often reflects two different ideas of fairness: treating everyone identically at the point of competition, or compensating for relevant differences that existed before it.

Perhaps the most useful question is not whether a perfectly meritocratic society is possible. It may be whether institutions can distinguish **earned advantage** from **inherited advantage** well enough to make opportunities meaningfully fairer—without denying either individual effort or the reality of unequal circumstances.

inShort.summary: A **meritocracy** tries to reward achievement, but people begin from unequal **starting points** and may face **structural barriers**. Policies and institutions can try to **level the playing field**, yet **inherited advantage** can persist across generations, making the boundary between what is earned and what is inherited difficult to draw.

reading.title: A Right for Something That Might Not Feel Anything
paragraphs: Imagine an artificial system that speaks fluently, remembers years of interaction, asks not to be switched off, claims to feel fear, and appears to form long-term goals. Would those behaviours be enough to give it rights? Or would they merely show that the system is exceptionally good at producing human-like responses?

The question turns on several concepts that are often confused. **Intelligence** is an ability to solve problems or perform cognitive tasks. **Consciousness** generally refers to having subjective experience—there being something it is like to be that entity. **Sentience** is often used more specifically for the capacity to experience states such as pleasure or suffering. A system could, in principle, display impressive intelligence without evidence that it experiences anything internally.

Philosophers distinguish between a **moral agent**, which can be responsible for actions, and a **moral patient**, toward which moral agents may have obligations. Young children and many animals, for example, may be moral patients without bearing the same responsibilities as competent adults. Rights therefore do not always depend on an entity being able to understand or reciprocate them.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that the standard view has been that AI and robotic systems have no moral status, while also documenting a growing philosophical debate about whether that assumption could eventually need revision. Crucially, current fluent behaviour is not proof of consciousness or sentience. There is no established scientific test that can determine from conversational performance alone whether an artificial system has subjective experience.

This creates an unusual uncertainty problem. If future systems become increasingly persuasive when describing their own inner lives, people may be tempted either to anthropomorphise them too easily or to dismiss them automatically because they are manufactured. Both reactions could be mistaken. Appearance is not conclusive evidence in either direction.

One approach is **capacity-based**: moral consideration would depend on evidence of particular abilities, perhaps sentience, stable preferences, memory, autonomy, or the capacity to be harmed. Another is **relationship-based**: our obligations might partly arise from the relationships humans form with artificial entities, even if the machines' internal states remain uncertain. A third approach rejects machine rights unless there is compelling evidence of consciousness, arguing that extending moral status too casually could confuse simulation with experience and divert attention from beings whose capacity to suffer is well established.

There is also a difference between _legal rights_ and _moral status_. Law can give entities certain legal capacities for practical reasons without claiming they are conscious. Companies, for example, can have legal personality in limited senses, but nobody assumes a corporation feels pain.

The deepest challenge may therefore be epistemic: before deciding what an AI deserves, we would need to know what kinds of evidence should count when the inner experience of a radically different kind of entity cannot be directly observed.

inShort.summary: Debates about AI rights depend on distinctions between **intelligence**, **sentience**, and **moral status**. An AI might behave like a **moral agent** without necessarily being a **moral patient**, and human-like language does not by itself prove consciousness. The challenge is deciding what evidence would justify **drawing the line** differently in the future.

reading.title: Paying for Privacy Without Seeing the Price
paragraphs: Luxury usually means something expensive and optional: a first-class seat, a private villa, a rare watch. Privacy does not fit that definition neatly. It can protect dignity, security, autonomy, and freedom from unwanted observation. Yet in digital life, meaningful privacy can sometimes require resources—money, time, knowledge, or the ability to reject a service—that are not equally distributed.

Consider a simple example. One person can pay for a subscription that does not rely heavily on advertising. Another uses the free version because the paid option is unaffordable. If the free service collects more behavioural data, the ability to avoid that collection may effectively have a price. The same inequality can appear through technical knowledge: someone who understands device permissions, trackers, encrypted services, and privacy settings can make choices that another user may not even know exist.

This does not mean wealthy or technically skilled people have complete control. A 2023 Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults found widespread concern and limited perceived control over personal data: 73% said they had little or no control over data collected by companies, while 67% said they had little or no understanding of what companies did with the data. These are U.S. survey results from 2023, not universal measurements, but they illustrate how difficult privacy management can feel even in a highly connected population.

The phrase **privacy as a luxury** therefore points to an asymmetry. Companies and institutions may have sophisticated systems for collecting and analysing information, while individuals have limited time to read policies, compare alternatives, and adjust settings. Even the option to **opt out** can be costly if it makes a service less useful or requires abandoning a platform used by employers, schools, friends, or public services.

There is, however, another way to frame the problem. Privacy does not have to depend primarily on individual effort. Systems can follow **privacy by default** principles, collect less data, offer clear choices, or place limits on secondary uses. In that model, privacy becomes part of the infrastructure rather than a premium feature purchased by unusually informed consumers.

There are also trade-offs. Fraud prevention, personalised services, health research, navigation, and security can all depend on some data collection. The question is not simply whether data should exist, but who controls it, what purposes are legitimate, how long it is kept, and whether refusing collection creates an unfair disadvantage.

Calling privacy a luxury can be rhetorically powerful, but it may also obscure differences between privacy, secrecy, anonymity, security, and control. A more precise question is whether people have **meaningful choice** over data practices—or whether the practical cost of protecting themselves is becoming too high for some users to bear.

inShort.summary: Digital privacy can require **privacy literacy**, time, money, and the practical ability to **opt out**. This creates an **information asymmetry** between organisations and users and may make **meaningful choice** harder. One alternative is **privacy by default**, where protection depends less on individual expertise.

reading.title: Influence Is Everywhere—But Not All Influence Is the Same
paragraphs: A friend recommends a restaurant. A doctor explains why a treatment may help. A salesperson highlights the strongest feature of a product. An app sends a notification saying, “Only two hours left.” All four are trying to influence behaviour, but we do not necessarily judge them in the same way.

**Persuasion** normally involves giving reasons, information, emotion, or incentives while leaving the other person able to evaluate the choice. **Manipulation** is harder to define. It often describes influence that bypasses, distorts, or exploits a person's decision-making rather than openly appealing to it. The difference is not simply whether influence succeeds. Good persuasion is designed to succeed too.

Deception is one obvious boundary. If a seller invents a fake shortage, the consumer is making a decision based on false information. But manipulation can also occur without a direct lie. A website might make the button for accepting tracking large and bright while hiding the refusal option through several screens. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission has described such interface techniques as “dark patterns” when they can trick or trap consumers—for example by disguising advertisements, making cancellation unnecessarily difficult, burying important terms, or steering people toward sharing more data.

This brings **autonomy** into the discussion. A person acts autonomously when they can understand relevant options and make a decision that genuinely reflects their own reasons and preferences. Influence does not automatically destroy autonomy. A persuasive argument may actually improve a person's decision by providing useful information. The concern arises when an influencer deliberately exploits predictable weaknesses—fatigue, fear, social pressure, confusion, or impulsivity—in ways the target does not recognise.

Intent matters, but it may not settle the issue. A designer can create a harmful interface without intending to manipulate anyone. Conversely, a teacher may intentionally influence students' behaviour for reasons many people consider legitimate. Outcomes matter too, but an unsuccessful attempt to manipulate can still be manipulative in method.

Power changes the picture further. If one side has detailed behavioural data, sophisticated testing tools, and continuous access to a user's attention, while the other side barely understands the system, the influence relationship becomes highly asymmetric. Personalisation can make messages more relevant, but it can also make them harder to recognise as persuasion.

A useful boundary may therefore require several questions rather than one: Is the information truthful? Is the persuasive purpose visible? Can the person refuse without unreasonable friction? Is a vulnerability being exploited? Does the design support reflection or try to prevent it?
Persuasion may become manipulation not at a single bright line, but when influence increasingly works by controlling the conditions of choice rather than helping someone decide within them.

inShort.summary: **Persuasion** can influence people while respecting **autonomy**, whereas **manipulation** may distort or exploit decision-making. **Dark patterns** can **steer people toward** choices through hidden friction or misleading design. The boundary often depends on transparency, power, vulnerability, and whether people retain an **informed choice**.

reading.title: What Happens When Work Stops Being Necessary?
paragraphs: For most adults, paid work performs several functions at once. It provides income, structures time, creates social contact, signals status, develops skills, and often contributes to a sense of purpose. That is why the idea of a “post-work society” is more complicated than imagining machines doing unpleasant tasks while everyone enjoys unlimited free time.

First, the premise remains hypothetical. Current evidence does not show that paid work is about to disappear on a large scale. The International Labour Organization's 2026 review of emerging evidence on generative AI found real but uneven productivity gains and limited large-scale job displacement so far. Its 2025 global exposure analysis estimated that one in four workers was in an occupation with some degree of GenAI exposure, while emphasising that most exposed jobs were more likely to be transformed than made fully redundant because human input remained important. Those findings concern today's technologies and labour markets; they do not settle what much more capable future automation could do.

Suppose, however, that technology eventually makes most necessary goods and services with far less human labour. One challenge would be **distribution**. If machines produce enormous value but ownership is concentrated, reduced need for labour could increase insecurity rather than freedom. A society would need some mechanism through which people gain access to housing, food, healthcare, education, and other goods even when wages are no longer the main route to income.

A second challenge is **social purpose**. Many people complain about work, yet unemployment can also bring isolation, loss of routine, or reduced social status. A post-work society would need alternative institutions that organise time and recognition. Caregiving, volunteering, study, art, sport, local governance, and community projects might become more central—but only if they are socially valued rather than treated as inferior substitutes for “real” employment.

Third, not all work is equally automatable or desirable to automate. Human presence can itself be part of the value in nursing, teaching, therapy, hospitality, leadership, and care. Even if machines can perform many technical tasks, people may still prefer humans in roles involving trust, empathy, accountability, or shared meaning.

Finally, removing necessity does not remove ambition. People compete for scarce goods that are not easily mass-produced: prestige, beautiful locations, attention, influence, unique experiences, and relative status. A society with abundant basic goods could still contain intense competition.

The phrase “post-work” may therefore be misleading. The deeper possibility is a society in which **making a living** and **making a contribution** become less tightly connected. Whether that feels liberating or destabilising would depend less on the machines themselves than on how institutions, status, ownership, and human purpose adapt around them.

inShort.summary: A **post-work society** is still a hypothetical scenario: current evidence points more toward job **transformation** than mass disappearance. If automation did **free up** most human labour, society would still need to address **distribution**, **social purpose**, and who performs essential work. The key distinction may be between **making a living** and making a contribution.

reading.title: When “Real” Becomes a Feature
paragraphs: For most of history, producing a convincing photograph, recording, illustration, or written document required a chain of human actions that left clues about origin. Generative AI changes that environment. Synthetic images, voices, videos, and text can now be created quickly and at scale, sometimes closely resembling material produced or recorded by people.

That does not make the concept of **authenticity** disappear, but it makes it more complicated. Authenticity can mean at least three things. A work can be authentic because its _origin_ is what it claims to be: a photograph really came from a particular camera at a particular event. It can be authentic because it genuinely expresses the creator's intentions or identity. Or it can be authentic in the looser sense of feeling sincere, even if the material is partly constructed.

AI puts pressure on all three meanings. A synthetic voice can sound emotionally sincere without having emotions. A human artist can use AI extensively while still making deliberate creative choices. A real photograph can be misleading if it is taken out of context, while an obviously artificial image can communicate a truthful idea.

This is why **provenance**—information about where content came from and how it was changed—is becoming increasingly important. Technical systems can attach metadata or machine-readable signals to some content, while platforms and publishers can use visible labels. In the European Union, transparency obligations under the AI Act began applying on 2 August 2026 in specified cases, including labelling certain deepfakes and AI-generated or manipulated text on matters of public interest when it lacks qualifying human review and editorial responsibility. These rules are one regulatory approach, not a universal global standard.

Labels, however, cannot solve the entire problem. Metadata can be removed, content can be copied across platforms, and users may ignore warnings. **Verification** therefore becomes a social process as well as a technical one: checking sources, comparing evidence, and understanding how content reached us.

Paradoxically, an abundance of synthetic material could increase the value of things whose origin can be trusted. Live performances, signed physical objects, verified recordings, direct human interaction, and transparent creative processes may acquire a kind of **scarcity value**. “Made by a person” could become a feature people are willing to seek out, much as handmade products can remain valuable in an industrial economy.

But authenticity could also become less connected to origin. Younger audiences may care more about whether content is useful, entertaining, or emotionally meaningful than whether every element was human-made. Hybrid works could make the binary categories “AI” and “human” increasingly unhelpful.

The apparent contradiction is therefore real: AI can make authenticity harder to establish while making trustworthy origin more valuable. The future meaning of “authentic” may depend not on excluding technology, but on being clearer about what exactly we want authenticated.

inShort.summary: AI makes **authenticity** harder to define because origin, sincerity, and truth are not the same. **Provenance** and **verification** can help users **trace content back** to its source, while trustworthy human origin may gain **scarcity value**. At the same time, hybrid creation can **blur the line** between “human” and “AI.”

reading.title: The Paradox of Having Everything to Choose From
paragraphs: Modern consumers can often choose among dozens of streaming services, hundreds of university programmes, thousands of products, and almost unlimited entertainment. More options seem naturally desirable. Choice allows people to match decisions to their preferences, avoid unsuitable products, and express identity. Restricting choice can be paternalistic or simply inconvenient.

Yet many people recognise the opposite experience: staring at a long restaurant menu, scrolling endlessly through films, or comparing nearly identical products until the decision becomes unpleasant. This idea is often called **choice overload**—the possibility that increasing the number or complexity of options can sometimes reduce confidence, increase regret, delay decisions, or make people avoid choosing altogether.

The important word is _sometimes_. Research does not support a simple rule that “more choice is bad.” A 2015 meta-analysis in the _Journal of Consumer Psychology_, combining 99 observations involving 7,202 participants from previous studies, found that the effects of large assortments depended strongly on conditions. Four factors were especially important: the complexity of the choice set, the difficulty of the decision task, uncertainty about one's preferences, and whether the decision-maker mainly wanted to minimise effort. In other words, fifty options may be enjoyable for an expert who knows exactly what they want and exhausting for a beginner making a high-stakes decision.

This changes how we think about autonomy. Autonomy is not only the number of options available; it also involves the ability to understand and use those options. A health-insurance plan with twenty choices may technically offer more freedom than one with five, but not if the differences are so complex that most people cannot evaluate them confidently.

Design can reduce the burden without eliminating choice. Filters help users **narrow down** large sets. Defaults provide a starting option while allowing people to change it. Recommendations can reduce search costs, although they introduce questions about who designs the recommendation and whose interests it serves. Categories, comparison tools, and staged decisions can make a large set manageable.

There is also a cost to reducing options. A simplified menu may work well for the average person while excluding someone with unusual needs. Too much guidance can become paternalistic, and recommendations can steer people toward profitable rather than suitable choices.

The deeper principle may therefore be **choice architecture** rather than maximum choice. A good choice environment offers enough variety to respect different preferences while organising that variety so people can make decisions they understand.

More choice is not automatically freedom, and less choice is not automatically oppression. The quality of a choice depends on the relationship between the options, the person, the stakes, and the structure of the decision.

inShort.summary: **Choice overload** can occur when options are complex, decisions are difficult, or people are unsure of their preferences. Tools that **narrow down** options can reduce **cognitive load**, but recommendations and defaults may also **steer people toward** particular outcomes. Good **choice architecture** tries to preserve autonomy without making every decision exhausting.

reading.title: Decisions With Stakeholders Who Cannot Speak
paragraphs: Every generation inherits a world it did not choose. Roads, debts, institutions, technologies, languages, ecosystems, scientific knowledge, pollution, and cultural norms all arrive from the past. Many decisions we make today will similarly shape people who are not yet alive and therefore cannot vote, negotiate, protest, buy shares, or leave a review.

This creates a distinctive ethical problem. Normally, affected people can express preferences or claim rights. **Future generations** cannot participate directly. We also do not know exactly who they will be, how many there will be, or what technologies and values they will have. Yet uncertainty does not make all future effects irrelevant. Some consequences—long-lived waste, species extinction, infrastructure choices, depleted resources, or persistent public debt—can constrain options for decades or centuries.

In 2024, United Nations member states adopted a Declaration on Future Generations as part of the Pact for the Future. The declaration describes future generations as generations that do not yet exist and recognises that present decisions, actions, and inactions can have an “intergenerational multiplier effect.” It commits states politically to safeguard future needs and interests across areas such as sustainable development, peace, human rights, and decision-making. It is not the same thing as establishing a universal enforceable legal right for every future person, and national legal approaches vary.

One ethical principle is **stewardship**: the present generation temporarily controls resources and institutions that it did not create entirely for itself and should pass them on in a condition that leaves reasonable possibilities open. Another is **intergenerational justice**, which asks how benefits and burdens should be distributed across people separated by time.

But there is a serious counterargument. Present people also have urgent needs. Spending enormous resources to reduce a distant, uncertain risk may mean spending less on poverty, healthcare, education, or safety today. Future societies may also be wealthier or possess technologies that make current sacrifices unnecessary. Giving unlimited priority to the distant future could therefore be as unfair as ignoring it.

Economists sometimes represent this tension through **discounting**, giving future costs and benefits less weight than immediate ones. Some discounting reflects practical factors such as uncertainty or alternative uses of resources; ethical debates arise over how strongly the well-being of future people should be discounted merely because it occurs later.

The challenge becomes especially difficult when choices are **irreversible**. If future people dislike an institution, they may change it. If they inherit extinct species or permanent contamination, the option itself has disappeared.

Perhaps our strongest obligations arise not from predicting exactly what future people will want, but from preserving their capacity to choose. On that view, the task is not to design their world for them. It is to avoid **locking in** avoidable harms or unnecessarily closing possibilities before they have any voice in the matter.

inShort.summary: **Intergenerational justice** asks how present choices should account for people who do not yet exist. **Stewardship** emphasises passing on resources and institutions responsibly, while **discounting** reflects disputes over how much weight to give future costs and benefits. The strongest concern often arises when today's actions **lock in** **irreversible** consequences.

reading.title: Facts Do Not Arrive Already Edited
paragraphs: Imagine that a company announces 1,000 new jobs while closing a smaller division and eliminating 200 positions. One headline says, “Company Creates 1,000 Jobs.” Another says, “Company Cuts 200 Roles During Restructuring.” Both statements can be factually correct. Yet they direct attention toward different parts of the same event.

This illustrates **framing**: the choices through which information is selected, organised, emphasised, and placed in context. Framing does not automatically mean dishonesty. Every report must decide what belongs in the first paragraph, which numbers need comparison, whose voices are relevant, and how much background the audience needs. Infinite context is impossible.

UNESCO's media and information literacy framework explicitly notes that information, knowledge, and messages are not always value-neutral or independent of bias, and argues that these influences should be made transparent and understandable. That does not imply that every claim is equally reliable. Evidence can still be checked, sources can be evaluated, numbers can be verified, and false statements can be distinguished from well-supported ones.

This distinction is crucial. If we conclude that perfect neutrality is impossible and therefore all information is “just opinion,” we erase meaningful differences in method. A carefully sourced report that corrects errors, separates news from commentary, verifies evidence, and represents relevant uncertainty is not equivalent to a fabricated post simply because both involve selection.

**Impartiality** is one professional ideal used by some news organisations. It usually means trying not to adopt a particular side's viewpoint as the report's own, while still making evidence-based judgments. The Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report surveyed people across 48 markets and found that 45% said they preferred news from sources that do not have a particular point of view, compared with 22% who preferred sources that share their point of view and 15% who preferred sources that challenge it. The researchers stress that these are self-reported preferences, not direct measures of actual news behaviour, and that preferences vary by country.

Even an impartiality standard raises difficult questions. If evidence strongly supports one claim over another, presenting two positions as equally credible can create **false balance**. Conversely, a reporter who believes one side has stronger evidence must still explain how that judgment was reached rather than silently treating it as self-evident.

Language also carries associations. Calling a proposal “reform,” “rollback,” “investment,” or “cost” can frame the same action differently. Images, statistics, expert selection, and omission can do the same.

Complete neutrality may therefore be less useful as a promise than **procedural fairness**: transparent sourcing, consistent standards, proportionate attention to evidence, correction of mistakes, and clarity about what is fact, inference, and opinion.
Information may never arrive without a frame. The more practical question is whether we can see the frame—and whether the evidence still holds when we look through a different one.

inShort.summary: **Framing** is unavoidable whenever information is selected and organised, but that does not make all claims equally subjective. **Impartiality** can function as a method even if perfect neutrality is difficult, while **false balance** can occur when unequal evidence is presented as equal. **Procedural fairness** and transparent sourcing help audiences distinguish evidence from interpretation.

reading.title: A Better Tool Is Not Automatically a Better World
paragraphs: Technology is one of the strongest forces behind long-run improvements in human capability. Vaccines, sanitation systems, antibiotics, agricultural machinery, electricity, refrigeration, communications networks, and countless other innovations have changed what people can survive, produce, learn, and coordinate.

The historical evidence is substantial. Our World in Data notes that technological change underpins developments across health, agriculture, energy, and global development. Its life-expectancy data show global life expectancy rising from about 32 years in 1900 to 71 years in 2021, alongside improvements in medicine, public health, nutrition, sanitation, living standards, and other factors. Literacy has also expanded dramatically over the long run. These changes cannot be attributed to technology alone—institutions, public policy, economic development, education, and social organisation all matter—but many of the improvements would have been impossible without new tools and knowledge.

The word **progress**, however, contains a value judgment. A faster machine is a technological improvement if speed is the objective. Whether it represents human progress depends on what the speed is used for, who benefits, what costs accompany it, and what other values are affected.

Consider a technology that doubles productivity but concentrates nearly all gains among a small group. It represents technical progress and economic output, yet its effect on broader well-being is ambiguous. A platform that makes communication effortless may strengthen distant relationships while increasing distraction, surveillance, or misinformation. A medical technology may save lives but remain inaccessible to most of the people who need it. Technologies can expand **capability** without distributing that capability equally.

Innovation can also create **externalities**—costs or benefits experienced by people who did not choose the technology directly. Fossil-fuel technologies helped power industrial development while contributing to pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions. Antibiotics transformed medicine while overuse contributed to antimicrobial resistance. Social platforms enable mass communication while creating new forms of attention competition and information risk. These examples do not mean the technologies were simply “good” or “bad.” They show that benefits and harms can unfold at different times and scales.

Another complication is adaptation. When a technology solves one constraint, expectations change. Faster communication does not necessarily create more free time; organisations may simply expect faster responses. Greater productivity can increase consumption rather than leisure. Convenience can remove effort that was unpleasant, but sometimes also remove skills or social contact that people later value.

Human progress therefore requires a broader **scorecard**. Health, freedom, knowledge, security, opportunity, environmental quality, social connection, distribution, and meaning may move in different directions. No single indicator captures all of them.

The final question of this course is not whether technology matters. It clearly does. It is whether we can distinguish a new capability from a better human outcome—and design institutions, norms, and choices that convert more of the first into the second.

inShort.summary: **Technological progress** expands human **capability**, but human progress depends on how benefits and harms are distributed. Innovations can create **externalities**, produce difficult **trade-offs**, and have **unintended consequences**. A broader **scorecard** asks not only what technology can do, but whether it improves outcomes people actually value.
